planting.note: Sow fresh seed in fall directly in place; Alba comes reliably true from seed as a pure-white strain and resents the root disturbance of transplanting once established.

directions: Alba is a pure-white-flowered selection of pasque flower, opening the same silky, goblet-shaped blooms as the species but in clean white with a bright central boss of golden stamens, set against finely cut, silvery-hairy foliage. Early spring bloom is followed by the genus's signature feathery, plumed seedheads, which extend ornamental interest for weeks after the petals drop. Give it perfectly drained, lean, gritty, neutral-to-alkaline soil in full sun, since wet or heavy ground is quickly fatal to the fleshy taproot. Sow fresh seed in fall, as pasque flower seed loses viability quickly and does not store well.

common_name: Eva Constance Pasque Flower (Compact Crimson Pulsatilla)

planting.note: Sow fresh seed in fall directly in place; this compact named selection is propagated by seed collected from true-to-type stock rather than by division.

directions: Eva Constance is a dwarf, neat-clumping pasque flower selection prized for its velvety, deep crimson-red flowers held low over a dense tuft of finely dissected, silky-haired leaves, making it especially suited to raised beds, scree, and trough plantings where its small scale would otherwise be lost among larger neighbors. Flowers open in earliest spring and are followed by the same decorative, silky-plumed seedheads common to the genus. As with all pasque flowers, it demands perfectly drained, lean, gritty soil in full sun and a position where its thick taproot will never need to be disturbed. Sow fresh seed in fall, since the seed deteriorates rapidly in storage.

planting.note: Sow fresh seed in fall directly where plants are to grow, since the seed needs a cold, moist winter to break dormancy and the thick taproot resents being moved once established.

directions: Eastern pasque flower is a true prairie species native to dry, open grasslands of the northern Great Plains, Rockies, and boreal regions, producing hairy, upright violet-blue to pale lavender cups among feathery, silver-haired, deeply cut foliage so early in spring that bloom often coincides with the last snowmelt. After flowering, the plant develops showy, silky, plume-tailed seed clusters that catch the light and persist for weeks, giving the plant a second season of ornamental interest. It demands lean, fast-draining, gravelly or sandy soil and full sun, mimicking the exposed prairie hillsides and rocky outcrops where it grows wild, and will rot in rich or poorly drained garden soil. Because of its deep taproot and dislike of disturbance, it is almost always grown from direct-sown seed rather than transplanted divisions.

planting.note: Plant nursery-propagated rhizome divisions in fall at the same depth they were growing, in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic woodland soil in partial to full shade; never collect this uncommon color form from the wild.

directions: This naturally occurring white-flowered form of red trillium substitutes clean, creamy-white petals for the species' usual maroon, while retaining the same dark, contrasting ovary at the flower's center and the same broad whorl of mottled green leaves, making it a striking and much sought-after variant among trillium collectors. It blooms at the same time as typical red trillium in mid-spring and shares its carrion-like scent, which still draws the flies and beetles that pollinate it despite the unexpected flower color. Grow it exactly as you would the species, in deeply humus-rich, evenly moist, slightly acidic soil beneath deciduous trees, and be patient, since rhizomes establish and bulk up slowly. Source plants only from specialist woodland-plant or trillium nurseries propagating from seed or division, never from wild-collected stock, as this form is uncommon in the wild and slow to increase.
